nodes.name: Mud-surface diatoms
nodes.desc: Microscopic algae living in the top millimetres of tidal mud. They feed many deposit-feeding animals when the flats are exposed.

nodes.name: Eelgrass
nodes.desc: A flowering seagrass of sheltered flats. Meadows give young animals cover, and shore crabs eat its seeds.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting algae carried in with the tide. Filter feeders such as cockles and mussels strain them from the water.

nodes.name: Mudsnail
nodes.desc: A tiny snail that grazes the muddy surface in huge numbers. It is eaten by shrimp and by wading birds.

nodes.name: Lugworm
nodes.desc: A burrowing worm that swallows sand and digests the organic matter in it. Its coiled casts are visible at low tide.

nodes.name: Ragworm
nodes.desc: A common mudflat worm that feeds on surface mud and organic particles. Fish, crabs and shorebirds hunt it.

nodes.name: Common cockle
nodes.desc: A shallow-burrowing bivalve that filters food from the water. Red knots and oystercatchers both take it.

nodes.name: Blue mussel
nodes.desc: Forms dense beds on the flats by attaching to each other and to hard bits of ground. A preferred food of eiders and oystercatchers.

nodes.name: Baltic tellin
nodes.desc: A small clam that lies buried in the mud and feeds at the surface. Red knots like this bivalve on European mudflats.

nodes.name: Brown shrimp
nodes.desc: A small shrimp that moves onto the flats to feed. Young plaice eat shrimp, and seals take them occasionally.

nodes.name: Shore crab
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats bivalves, worms, small crustaceans and eelgrass seeds. It will also eat other crabs.

nodes.name: European plaice
nodes.desc: Young plaice settle on shallow flats and stay for a few months before moving to deeper water. They eat shrimp, then worms and bivalves.

nodes.name: Red knot
nodes.desc: Probes for buried shellfish and swallows them whole. It breeds on Arctic tundra and stops over on coastal mudflats such as the Wadden Sea.

nodes.name: Bar-tailed godwit
nodes.desc: A long-billed shorebird that eats mostly worms, with some bivalves and crustaceans. It breeds in the Arctic and winters along coasts of Europe and Africa.

nodes.name: Eurasian oystercatcher
nodes.desc: Uses its strong bill to open cockles and mussels or to dig up worms. Despite its name, oysters are not a major food.

nodes.name: Common eider
nodes.desc: A diving sea duck that swallows mussels whole and crushes them in its gizzard. It also eats crabs and other crustaceans.

nodes.name: Herring gull
nodes.desc: An opportunistic gull of the coast that feeds on shore crabs and other items found on the flats.

nodes.name: Harbour seal
nodes.desc: Rests on sandbanks at low tide. Eats mainly fish, including flatfish, and occasionally shrimp and crabs.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light reaching the exposed flats at low tide lets mud-surface algae and eelgrass grow.

nodes.name: Nutrients
nodes.desc: Nitrogen and phosphorus carried in from rivers and the sea. Bacteria in the mud release them again from dead matter.

nodes.name: Tides
nodes.desc: Twice daily the sea floods and uncovers the flats, setting feeding times for birds, fish and shellfish.

nodes.name: Mud bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead algae, plants and animals in the mud and return nutrients to the water.
